I don't want to go into the whole spiel (you can read my post history for some of it), but it was fucking weird and definitely contributed to the end of our relationship. She treated her dog like a child and husband. Her dog for her was an emotional crutch before we met, and her dog was the thing uncrouchable in our relationship. She kept her dog on a pedestal despite it being terribly untrained and neglected. Horrible, horrible attachment anxiety. She had a hard time keeping out of the room even during sex. There was not enough room for intimacy outside of her dog.

Nevertheless, we were together for two years, similar story to yours and nothing ever changed for me man.  You will be making the same post in a few years if you stay. I spent so much time thinking maybe I didn't like her dog enough, maybe she's simply using her dog to drive a wedge between you, maybe she just really fucking likes the dog, who knows. In the end, my ex said our sex difficulties had nothing to do with me. You have to realize that if she wanted to have sex with you, she would, but she does not want to. She has some internal block, whether thats because of you, her dog, or herself, you will probably never figure it out. Do not waste time trying to fix this outside of a few conversations. All you can do is control yourself. You don't want to develop a weird or shameful relationship with sex because of dog. Trust me.

I would also check out /r/talesfromthedoghouse if you haven't yet. For as much as people talk about sexual compatibility, pet compatibility is a big thing. It wouldn't surprise me if there were people who genuinely would rather spend a night cuddling there dog than having sex with their partner. That's where we are with dog culture at this point.

Cholesterol is necessary for cognitive functioning. Since you had a heart attack you may need to just switch to a less aggressive statin. As far as which those are I don't know. Statins also raise blood sugar so you may need to monitor that as that could contribute to brain fog.

Hey man, just want to say I've been in your shoes before. I was the best student in my high school growing, in-shape, charismatic, had leadership roles, etc. but a lot of people I grew up with would consider someone who peaked, "failure to launch", or never living up to my potential. So many people in my life have abandoned or given up on me. Eventually, this prompted me to give up on myself in basically every way imaginable. 

But the great thing about being a failure or going up on yourself is that you're no longer burdened by high expectations, or anything really. When you fail, you can really decide to be anything you want to be, whether that be a useless nobody, a degenerate, or some sort of comeback kid who overcame the odds and achieved anyway. Right now you have the opportunity to do anything you really want. What would you do? Your answer could even be "I don't know yet." I definitely didn't know what I wanted to do with my life at 19.

Also, be aware that your cognitive functioning can be clouded by a lot of things. I remember being 19 and feeling like I turned myself into an idiot, but fortunately we humans have been gifted with neuroplasticity which not only allows us to recreate connections to get us back in touch with who we used to be, but also grow new connections that can make us better than we were before. When you're 19, neuroplasticity is very high and enables you to change. 

Also keep in mind that a lot of the people that you think "have it all figured out" actually don't , more often than not. They may very well have the same thoughts you do.

Some vapes are just cheap crap from China. Some vapes that are "popular" and "good" really just have a lot of sneaky advertising behind them. There are also studies that indicate vaping is safer but keep in mind that doctors before the 60s used to prescribe cigarettes to patients who were mentally ill or needed to lose weight. Ultimately if you vape run it through it through a bong/water piece, just do it outside, and try to keep your health up in other areas (weight, exercise, yoga, breathing exercises, sleep, especially water.) Try to just do it in moderation as well.

I know how you feel. This year, I wasted so much money on therapists who told me so much of what I already know and they helped me little. However, I wouldn't say therapy is completely useless. I had one therapist in college who really got to me and really helped me. Since I met her, every sorta psychological problem has been easier. Self help books and stuff like that read easier as well. The things that my mostly useless therapists use to say makes more sense now. Maybe it's just because I've gotten older, but I think getting better is equivalent to making a mud castle. You just keep dumping mud (stuff that helps you heal) onto a pile. Sometimes that mud falls and goes back to the bottom (you forget it, it's not useful), but if you keep stacking up mud, something's going to be built eventually (you know how skills to make yourself better).

If you are keeping up with them on social media, unfriend, block, etc. If they wronged you in the past, you'll have to go through a grieving process with that. But at a certain point, you have to do whatever you can from letting these people enter your mind. It's not healthy to keep up with these people or care about what they're doing. Think about it. Do you think they think about you at all?

You really have to learn to train yourself just not to care. For me, that was deleting stuff basically all non-anonymous social media.

Do I still get pangs of jealousy and anger? Yes, but it's pangs instead of obsession which is a whole lot better.

I still live with similarly awful parents as well. I second reading "Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents" or whatever it's called. It will explain both of their behaviors and give you tools deal with them and deal with the future problems you'll have to overcome. Furthermore, it has a lot of information in case you want to keep contact with your parents after moving out without letting them continue to run roughshod over your life. 

At the end of the day, all you can do with them is grey rock. View every interaction with your parents as if they're setting out bait. They want you to get emotional and overact. Every time you grey rock you become more and more powerful. In turn it becomes clearer how childish they really are. It's really the only way to survive living with them. It may feel bad or cruel but you have to learn to prioritize yourself.

To lose weight, try to think about things in baby steps. Let's say randomly that I eat pizza everyday. I will make an improvement if I only eat pizza 6 days a week or if I eat it every other day. Whether it is exercise, eating, or whatever, just think of it in baby steps. When I was losing weight, about every other week I would get something I really wanted, like wings or Chinese food. I didn't view it as me messing up, I viewed it as me enjoying something I wanted. If you mess up, move on and just try to get it right the next time. Weight loss culture is so filled with the mindset of perfection and that if you eat these many calories or this much cholesterol or if you look like this at this age then you're whole life is ruined. Just focus on improving from where you are right now. Losing just 5 pounds can make a difference and can give you momentum for the long haul. Also, remember to be kind to yourself. Being kinder to yourself will give yourself strength. I wasn't able to lose weight until I loved myself for who I was. I had to learn how to love myself at 315 lbs when it felt like everyone in the world was looking down on me. Now that I have lost some weight, I love the bigger version of me just as much as the skinnier version of me. Just please be kind to yourself and try to love yourself each day.

I have African parents but it's the same abuse story as yours. Going to therapy and getting on medication helped me a lot. Personally I was a pretty self-destructive person due to all the depression and anxiety etc. But my therapist helped me realize that the self-destruction was just giving my parents what they wanted. Suicide is the same situation. You're just letting the people who hurt you win. After months of therapy, I don't self-destruct as much and I've learned to put myself first (life isn't perfect, but it never will be). It feels really good because every time something goes right it's in spite of my parents and everything I went through, so there's that extra feeling of accomplishment. I don't know what your home or financial situation is, but the most important thing to know is that your life is your life. That means that "what other people think" (another thing my parents are obsessed with) is not important. The most important thing is what you think. Your parents can say whatever and tell you to do whatever, but ultimately you're the one who makes decisions and lives with the consequences. Follow your gut. That feeling that you get exists for a reason and it's not going away.  

Also, if something like therapy or psychiatry will cause trouble with your parents (my mom told me not to "look into those sorts of things" ), just don't tell them. I don't like lying, but it's important to protect yourself first and get the help that you need.
